name: Medical Affairs and Medical Writing
blurb: AI in regulatory and medical writing, evidence dossiers, study reports and promotional review.
title: Medical Affairs and Medical Writing
answer: Medical writers use generative AI to draft and summarise clinical study reports, submission modules and evidence dossiers, and to speed promotional review. Regulators have set no separate pathway for AI written content: the sponsor stays fully accountable for every word submitted.

reading.body:
Medical writers use generative AI for first drafts and summaries, but no regulator has created a separate pathway for AI written content, so the sponsor remains accountable for every word submitted.

The pattern across the sub-topics is consistent: AI enters at the drafting stage, in clinical study reports, submission modules, evidence dossiers and promotional review, while accountability stays with the sponsor. The FDA's draft guidance on AI in drug development keeps responsibility for submitted information with the sponsor and asks for evidence of model credibility where AI produces regulatory data. A review in Clinical and Translational Science reached the same practical conclusion, that human review remains essential.

For AI specifically, this is a governance constraint rather than a compute one. The bottleneck in medical writing is not model capability but traceability, since every statement must trace to source data and the review trail must show who checked it. Citation reliability is a named concern, which is why the working rule is first drafts, summaries and consistency checks, never final authorship.

What the data does not cover is volume. It gives no count of submissions drafted with AI, no error or retraction rates, and no comparison of AI assisted writing against conventional drafting. It also does not say how regulators will treat AI use in practice beyond the sponsor accountability principle, or whether any submission has been rejected over it.

terms.line: The field of computer science dedicated to creating systems that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence: understanding language, recognizing patterns, making decisions.

Models that create new content, text, images, video, audio, code, from patterns learned in training data. The 2022 shift from AI that classifies to AI that produces is what put this glossary on your reading list.

explainer:
Medical affairs and medical writing produce the scientific documents that carry a medicine through development and onto the market: clinical study reports, the summaries in a regulatory submission, investigator brochures, evidence dossiers for payers, publications, and the medical information that answers doctors' questions. These documents are long, highly structured and must be exactly consistent with the underlying data.

That structure makes them well suited to AI assistance. Generative models can assemble draft sections from statistical tables and protocols, summarise large evidence sets, check consistency across documents, screen literature for systematic reviews, and pre-check promotional material for missing safety statements or prohibited claims. Published studies report large time savings on specific drafting tasks.

The risks are equally specific. Language models can misstate numbers, omit qualifications or invent references, and an error in a regulatory document can delay an approval or mislead prescribers. No regulator offers a separate route for AI written content: the sponsor is accountable for every word, and where AI produces data a regulator relies on, its credibility must be shown.

Good practice therefore keeps AI on drafting, summarising and checking, generates text only from validated sources, verifies every number and citation against the original, and keeps a named author and reviewer responsible for each section.
key_points: Regulatory and medical documents are structured and data bound, which suits AI drafting.
AI helps with drafting, summarising, consistency checks, literature screening and review pre-checks.
Models can misstate figures and invent references, so verification is mandatory.
Sponsors remain fully accountable for AI assisted content.
